title: Generic STL Surface Cutting
overview: Cut a closed STL triangle shell between two user-defined planar sections without using analytic shape definitions. The canonical internal-flow cylinder STL is the first blind-input fixture. The oblique-cut cylinder fixture verifies an elliptical inlet generated by a 30-degree plane cut while retaining a circular outlet.
principle: The STL triangles are the sole geometry source. The cutter must not read analytic geometry manifests, primitive parameters, patch indices or shape equations. Inlet and outlet planes are explicit inputs; their normals orient the retained half-spaces and the generated end caps. A blind-input cylinder fixture cuts its inlet with a 30-degree oblique plane; the ellipse is measured from the resulting boundary loop rather than inferred from an analytic geometry manifest.
architecture: grid/stl_import/surface_cut.py (Python reference) and codes/geometry/stl (native C++) -> generic plane clipping, boundary-loop reconstruction and cap triangulation -> closed STL plus wall/inflow/outflow regions -> region-preserving Gmsh CreateTopology/CreateGeometry -> Physical Surfaces + fluid_domain -> MSH 4.1 -> CGNS -> OneFLOW native grid.

algorithm: Provide STL mesh IO, topology analysis and plane cutting as a reusable native Geometry submodule under codes/geometry/stl.
Expose the native operation through GridConfig parameters; stlSurfaceCutEnabled defaults to false and stlSurfaceCutConfigFile selects the plane configuration.
Use the same case-level cutting-plane JSON for native C++ and Python reference execution; the algorithm consumes only STL triangles and plane parameters.
Validate a connected, closed, consistently oriented two-manifold input shell.
Clip each triangle polygon against the inlet and outlet plane half-spaces using signed distances.
Weld clipped vertices and extract one-use boundary edges on each cutting plane.
Require one simple closed loop per plane.
Project each loop into a local plane basis and triangulate it using ear clipping.
Orient inlet and outlet cap triangles outward and combine them with the clipped side surface.
Write a checksum-bound region manifest for wall, inflow and outflow STL artifacts; do not infer regions from analytic geometry.
Copy the manifest and its patch STL files into the writable mesh project when the closed shell is opened in STL to Gmsh.
Create distinct Gmsh Physical Surface groups named wall, inflow and outflow and a fluid_domain Physical Volume.

Use the 30-degree inlet-plane cylinder fixture to verify that an oblique plane/cylinder intersection produces an elliptical inlet loop (major/minor ratio approximately 1.1547) while the perpendicular outlet remains circular.
Pass the clipped and capped STL plus checksum-bound region manifest through the region-aware Gmsh converter and verify non-empty wall/inflow/outflow/fluid_domain Physical Groups.
Register the generated oblique-cut MSH as an existing-mesh validation input; hand it to the shared Gmsh-to-CGNS-to-OneFLOW-to-CFD workflow without rerunning the mesh producer.
limitations: One boundary loop per cutting plane.
Plane points and normals are supplied explicitly; automatic endpoint direction estimation is not included.
The automated curved-surface integration fixture is a cut prolate shell; it validates the two-loop wall topology but is not a replacement for the user's exact pipe geometry.
The native C++ cutter currently requires one connected, closed, outward-oriented input shell and one simple loop at each cutting plane.
Native C++ cut-region Physical Group preservation is available only through the region-aware closed-surface Gmsh pipeline; CGNS-only surface conversion does not preserve the three named cut patches.
The current closed-surface Gmsh volume path requires genus-zero topology; handles or multiple boundary loops are rejected.
Zero-area and near-degenerate input triangles are rejected during topology analysis.
The native parameter path rejects non-3-D layouts and volume pipelines other than closed_surface_automatic_tetrahedra.

execution_boundary.ci: CI runs the generic STL cut and Gmsh 4.15.2 volume-mesh integration on Linux and Windows. The Windows OneFLOW workflow additionally converts the generated MSH through CGNS into a native OneFLOW unstructured grid and requires the subsequent oneflow_cfd_solve smoke stage to pass. The existing laminar flat-plate solver controls are reused with the runtime dimension overridden to 3D; this is a solver smoke test, not a physical-accuracy claim.
execution_boundary.manual: For a user-provided geometry, review the selected cut planes and the generated geometry. Physical CFD validation remains a separate task requiring a compatible internal-flow Case, explicit boundary-state data and physical acceptance criteria.
